13176-the-abolitionists-together-with-pe:
John F. Hume's 1905 Abolitionists, with personal memories of the struggle for human rights from 1830 to 1864, opens with Theodore Roosevelt and the abolitionists. Chapters cover who they were, pro-slavery prejudice, pioneers, Chase, John Quincy Adams, societies, orators, Lincoln and Douglas, women, mobs, martyrs, and the Underground Railroad. Hume writes from memory and study alike.

He stresses that Lundy and Garrison had little to lose, but James Gillespie Birney, a southerner of wealth and schooling, risked far more. A later passage tells of a plan to move the whole Black race to Texas as a republic, a dream that never came to pass. Hume's book is a tribute to unpopular courage, and a useful survey of the movement's people.
13211-the-pearl-a-middle-english-poem-a-:
Sophie Jewett, associate professor at Wellesley, published this modern version of the Middle English poem Pearl in 1908, keeping the metre of the original. Jewett dedicates it to Katharine Lee Bates and apologizes in verse to the unknown poet, lest her touch tarnish the pearl's pure luster. Notes cite Morris and Gollancz editions and Dante.

The poem follows a jeweler who lost his pearl, a child, and meets her in a bright land beyond waves, where she speaks as a gem and queen. She chides his three unconsidered sayings: that she is truly there, that he may dwell with her, and that he may cross freely. Later, Christ's words on innocents frame the pearl as heaven's kingdom, bought dear. Jewett's version is musical, faithful, and moving.
14312-what-all-the-world-s-a-seeking-the:
Ralph Waldo Trine wrote this book on the vital law of true life, greatness, power, and happiness. Trine says two reasons moved him: the time was ripe, and his soul longed to speak on the theme. The book comes from the heart, he writes, and hopes to reach the heart. It teaches that man is a spiritual being, and that the higher self must rule the lower. Trine's prose is plain and full of uplift.

Trine shows a railway car changed by two travelers, till light hearts and voices fill it. True politeness, he says, springs from a life alone, and makes the gentleman: gentle, kind, and courteous by nature. As the God-self takes charge, life grows simple, and small trials fall away of their own accord. The reader feels, Trine writes, a thrill of the life universal. The book offers a gospel of self-rule.
14554-an-explanation-of-the-baltimore-ca:
The Reverend Thomas L. Kinkead wrote this Explanation of the Baltimore Catechism, known as No. 4, for Sunday-school teachers and advanced classes, first approved in 1891 and reissued with a 1921 imprimatur. It expands the shorter catechisms.

Kinkead explains each question with examples, such as a merchant who leaves an agent in charge to illustrate Christ's invisible headship of the Church through Peter. The volume covers doctrine, morals, and worship in full. It served teachers who needed more than the children's answers, and it remains a standard reference for the Baltimore tradition.
17000-of-the-orthographie-and-congruitie:
Alexander Hume wrote this short treatise on the spelling and fitness of the British tongue, for schools, edited by Henry B. Wheatley from the original manuscript in the British Museum and issued for the Early English Text Society by Trubner in London in 1865. Wheatley's preface says the tract is now printed for the first time from the old Royal Collection manuscript.

Hume sets out rules for Scots spelling and grammar in the quaint, earnest style of his age, with Greek words transliterated for modern readers. The tract gives a rare glimpse of how Scots writers thought about their own tongue. Readers of Scots language history will find a valuable primary text, short, exact, and full of period charm.
30105-the-strand-magazine-vol-05-issue-2:
The Strand Magazine for February 1893, volume 5, issue 26, leads with a wife's story, A Wedding Gift, by Leonard Outram. Its narrator recalls Kenneth Moore, who courted her since childhood and pressed his suit with dark threats, vowing to have her though he must fight a hundred men. Left alone by her mother's death, she promised him marriage, until Phillip Rutley came to the village and she fell in love with him instead.

An illustration shows Kenneth throwing himself suddenly upon Phillip, and the illustrated monthly format frames the tale with pictures throughout. The Strand, known for popular fiction in a handsome monthly package, gives the story room to breathe as a confession of love, fear, and choice. Readers of Victorian magazine fiction will find the number a vivid sample of its melodrama.
30660-discourses-on-a-sober-and-temperat:
Lewis Cornaro, a noble Venetian, writes Discourses on a Sober and Temperate Life. Translated from the Italian original in a new edition, corrected, it was printed in London in 1779 for Benjamin White at Horace's Head in Fleet Street. Cornaro demonstrates by his own example a method of preserving health to extreme old age.

A treatise on a sober life opens by noting that custom, over time, becomes a second nature. It forces men to use what they are habituated to, good or bad, and habit often beats reason. Virtuous men among the wicked may fall into vice, while bad morals may change again to good. Cornaro argues that temperate eating and living can restore and preserve health.
32015-a-historic-sketch-lest-we-forget-c:
Captain Welden Kelly wrote this historic sketch of Company E, 26th Ohio Volunteer Infantry, in the War for the Union from 1861 to 1865. Its title, Lest We Forget, states its purpose: to keep the company's men in memory. The company began at Mt. Gilead in Morrow County, Ohio, where Sylvester M. Hewitt began enlisting volunteers about June 5, 1861, under the President's first call for three-year troops.

Within days, local women had prepared woollen underwear for the men. On June 14, 1861, about eighty men formed on the North Public Square, marched to Gilead Station, and boarded a train for Columbus. From there they marched four miles west to Camp Chase, where three other Ohio regiments were also forming. Readers get a company history built from enlistment, camp life, and the shared memory of men who served together.
32656-letter-from-monsieur-de-cros-who-w:
Monsieur de Cros writes to a lord in answer to Sir William Temple's memoirs of the years 1672 to 1679. De Cros served as envoy at the Treaty of Nimeguen and as resident in England under King Charles II, and he says Temple slights him while praising himself.

The letter disputes Temple's claim to a large share in the king's secret designs, and it picks apart his account of talks at the Hague, Brussels, and Aix-la-Chapelle. It is a sharp, first-person rebuttal, keen to set the record of peace talks straight.
32695-women-of-medi-val-france-woman-in-:
Pierce Butler of Tulane University traces the place of women in medieval France. His book is volume five of the Woman in All Ages series, published by George Barrie and Sons in 1907. He opens under the Capetian kings, when chroniclers recorded battles and crimes and left women almost unnoticed.

Feudal order rested on military service, and that order gave women little recognized place. Later chapters follow queens and noblewomen who raised treasure, provisioned armies, and defended family claims in war and at court. Butler argues that history has been unjust to women most of all in this period. He recovers their work from chronicles, epics, and records that mention them only in passing.
33357-reminiscences-of-the-thirty-fourth:
William H. Clark's Reminiscences of the Thirty-Fourth Regiment, Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry, published for the author in 1871, recalls a Civil War regiment from a private's view. Clark, private of Company E, inscribes his sketches to General William S. Lincoln of Worcester, long and honorably linked to the regiment. He warns that his little work does not claim to be a full history.

The book's value lies in its modest, first-hand sketches, telling what one soldier saw and felt rather than what generals planned. Its tone is plain and comradely, suited to veterans and their kin. For readers of regimental history, it is a warm, useful record of the Thirty-Fourth's service, told by a man who marched with it.
35122-portrait-and-biography-of-parson-b:
Portrait and Biography of Parson Brownlow is a wartime pamphlet biography, sold at twenty five cents. Asher of Indianapolis issued it in 1862, in the second year of the Civil War. Brownlow is styled the Tennessee patriot on the title page in bold type. His last editorial in the Knoxville Whig is printed with the life.

Recent speeches rehearse his experience with secession and his prison life under it. An introduction praises great actions and calls him a patriot exile of modern times. Union readers in the north bought such lives to hearten the cause in war. The pamphlet preserves a fighting parson editor at the height of his fame.
35554-a-voice-of-warning-or-an-introduct:
A Voice of Warning is an introduction to the faith of the Latter-day Saints. Parley Pratt wrote the book, one of the church's early voices. The Deseret News Company printed this eleventh edition in 1881. Salt Lake City, Utah, stands as the place of that late printing. Lines from Isaiah head the title page as the book's warrant.

The first chapter treats prophecy already fulfilled in the world's story. Pratt lays down a rule for reading Scripture before he argues on. No prophecy is of private interpretation, he quotes from Peter's letter. Without such a rule the mind is lost in doubt, he warns. Holy men of old spoke as the Spirit moved them, he holds. The book instructs all people in the doctrine of the young church. Its title promises warning and instruction to every reader alike.
37930-the-legendary-and-poetical-remains:
John Roby won his reputation with Traditions of Lancashire, a famous set of legends of his county. After his early death, his widow gathered his Legendary and Poetical Remains and published them in London in 1854. A portrait from a daguerreotype stands at the front. Her preface explains that most of the poems and tales were finished for publication by Roby himself.

The widow also wrote the sketch of his literary life and character that opens the volume. A life so private, she admits, afforded few materials. She drew on his own memoranda and on the reminiscences of friends. She fears she has given too much space to what is personal to herself. The volume joins memoir, poems, and legendary tales as a widow's monument.
39464-macmillan-co-s-catalogue-april-188:
Macmillan and Company issued this catalogue of their works in belles lettres from Bedford Street, Covent Garden, in April 1888. Poetry, fiction, and gift books fill the list, sorted by author from A to Z, each with its size and price. The Golden Treasury Series appears again and again at four shillings and sixpence. Green's selections from Addison open the alphabet.

The author of John Halifax, Gentleman offers a gift book called About Money, a brownie tale for children, and a fairy tale, all in print at once. Caldecott's Aesop, with new translations by his brother, sells in a cheaper issue at five shillings. Amiel's journal, in the translation by Mrs Humphry Ward, takes two volumes at twelve shillings. As a snapshot of a great house's trade list in the late 1880s, the catalogue shows what polite England was expected to read.
40145-the-foolish-almanak-for-anuthur-ye:
The Foolish Almanak for Anuthur Year, by Theodor Rosyfelt, was copyrighted in 1906 and published at Boston by Luce. Pictures by Wallace Goldsmith attend the jokes. A mock perpetual pass on the first leaf runs from Worryland to Laughter, good till doomsday. The title boasts two novelties of the season: the introduction of the muck-rake in magazine gardening, and the spelling reform of the language.

The whole book is set in reformed spelling, played for laughs. There have been other years, it announces, but none like this: 313 days will come and 313 days will go. By kind permission of the Rockefellers, the sun and moon will be permitted to arise and shine. A helpful hint for January warns against vain regrets over broken resolves. The almanak spoofs Roosevelt-era fads, from simplified spelling to muckraking magazines.
42633-the-strand-magazine-vol-01-issue-0:
Strand Magazine for February 1891 is the second issue of the famous illustrated monthly. Contents open with The Pistol Shot, from the Russian of Alexander Pushkin. A night with the Thames police and the maid of Treppi follow in the bill. Our money manufactory shows readers where their coins and notes are made.

Portraits of celebrities at different times of their lives began a Strand signature feature. Letters from artists on ladies dress and actors dressing rooms fill the middle pages. A passion in the desert and the minister crime close the fiction list. Collectors prize this early number of the magazine that later made Sherlock Holmes.
45235-magic-stage-illusions-and-scientif:
Magic: Stage Illusions and Scientific Diversions is a fat handbook compiled by Albert Hopkins, printed at London in 1897. Hopkins edited a Scientific American cyclopedia of receipts and queries. Henry Ridgely Evans wrote the introduction. Four hundred pictures fill the pages, and trick photography has its own place.

The preface says most books of magic slight the big stage illusions. Here they stand first, with their secrets told. Optics, mechanics, sound, and electricity all serve the modern conjurer. Many explanations came from the performers themselves. Early chapters give the best illusions of Robert-Houdin, Professor Pepper, Herrmann, and Kellar, each shown plainly enough for a reader to follow.
47373-the-strand-magazine-vol-07-issue-3:
The Strand Magazine's thirty-eighth issue, dated February 1894, opens the magazine's seventh volume. George Newnes edited the Strand, the great London illustrated monthly. A front picture shows a woman clutching a fatal telegram, a pointer to a story inside at page 116.

The issue leads with Between the Acts, a tale translated from the French of Blowitz. It is set in 1870, when war had just been declared. Paris fetes the expected victory while MacMahon crosses the frontier. A young actress prepares her debut in La Dame aux Camelias on a boulevard stage. The Strand mixed such fiction with interviews, puzzles, and pictures, and in these years it was also printing the Sherlock Holmes stories that made it famous.
49476-thoughts-on-general-and-partial-in:
Thoughts on General and Partial Inoculations is Baron Thomas Dimsdale's plea for spreading smallpox inoculation among the poor. Dimsdale was first physician and actual counsellor of state to the Empress of all the Russias. The book was printed in London in 1776 and sold at one shilling and sixpence, addressed to the legislature of Great Britain.

It translates two treatises Dimsdale wrote at Petersburg, published there in Russian by command of her Imperial Majesty. The Empress, he says, was solicitous to render inoculation general among her subjects while England, fifty years after the practice arrived, left the poor to the bills of mortality. Two plans are outlined: one for the general inoculation of the poor in small towns and villages, another for London and other large and populous places. Private charity and the interposition of the legislature are his instruments.
49898-personal-record-of-the-thirteenth-:
A J Vaughan, old commander of the Thirteenth Tennessee Infantry, writes his regiment's record for its survivors. S C Toof and Company printed it at Memphis in 1897. The price was seventy-five cents. He dedicates it to the mothers and wives of his men.

His preface speaks straight to his old comrades. Writing carried him back to the morning time of his life. Cannon, musketry, and the old rebel yell sound again in his ears. He grants a shade of sorrow over the lost cause. Yet he denies any sorrow born of regret. The men who wore the gray, he says, took their parole in good faith. They stand now as loyal citizens of the United States. Such regimental records kept names and marches from vanishing.
51131-a-voyage-to-spitzbergen-containing:
John Laing, a surgeon, wrote this account of a voyage to Spitzbergen, in a new edition printed at Edinburgh in 1825. The book treats the zoology of the north, the Shetland Isles and the whale fishery. Laing inscribes the work to McCulloch as a testimony of esteem and gratitude at the front.

The journal Laing kept aboard the Resolution in 1806 forms the basis of the work. Observations from 1807 are worked into the narration as well, his advertisement explains. An appendix gives the history of the Dutch, English and American whale fisheries, with notes on the compass and extracts from Scoresby's paper on polar ice.
53373-a-manual-of-historic-ornament-trea:
A Manual of Historic Ornament, by Richard Glazier, treats the growth of design in building and the applied arts. Batsford printed the book in London in 1899, with four hundred and seventy drawings by the author. Glazier headed the Municipal School of Art at Manchester.

The book was made for students and craftsmen, and the preface states a threefold aim. It gives a basic knowledge of building and ornament, and it wakes a feeling for the fine remains of old cultures. Last, it points learners to the beauty and life of the industrial arts of the past. Glazier ties ornament to the social and religious life of each age. Line drawings serve better than pictures here, he says, since they show how a design is built. A list of reference books closes the manual.
54702-a-translation-of-octavia-a-latin-t:
A Translation of Octavia, a Latin Tragedy, with Notes and Introduction, by Elizabeth Twining Hall, is a master's thesis from the University of Illinois, approved in 1901. A certificate from the head of the Latin department signs off the work. The play is the Roman tragedy of Octavia, divorced wife of the emperor Nero.

Octavia opens the play lamenting her mother, her murdered father Claudius, and the stepmother who brought Stygian fires to her bridal room. Seneca, Poppaea, Agrippina, and a chorus share the stage. Hall's notes guide a student reader through the Latin world's most domestic imperial tragedy.
54967-anecdotes-of-the-american-indians-:
Anecdotes of the American Indians was printed in Hartford in 1850, from sheets first entered for copyright in 1843. The unnamed author had also written Evenings in Boston. His aim, set out in the preface, was to gather scattered tales of Native character into one small volume.

Short tales show courage, wit, grief, and revenge among the first peoples of North America. One early plate shows Weatherford's revenge. The author argues that Native traits had to be pieced together from lone tales and reports, since no full account existed. Modern readers will find the views dated, yet the book shows how white readers of its day pictured Native life.
57168-the-land-beyond-the-forest-facts-f:
Gerard wrote this travel book on Transylvania, issued by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1888, with a map and pictures. The title means what it says: Transylvania is the land beyond the forest. Her husband, an officer, took command of a cavalry brigade there in the spring of 1883, with regiments at Hermanstadt and Kronstadt, and she went gladly.

Two years in the country gave her the matter of the book: facts, figures, and fancies, as her subtitle promises. She writes of Saxon towns, Romanian villages, and the wild tales of the hills. Her pages on vampires and local lore fed the English taste that Bram Stoker would soon serve. The book is a bright, full record of a land then little known.
57292-echoes-from-the-orient-a-broad-out:
Echoes from the Orient is a broad outline of theosophical doctrines by William Judge, in an edition issued at Point Loma in 1910. The book was first entered for copyright in 1890, the front pages show. Judge writes under a Latin pen name meaning hidden on the title page. A publisher's book list at the back was updated by hand to mark titles out of print.

The second Point Loma edition keeps that lived in detail, notes a transcriber at the front. Judge set out to give the main lines of theosophical teaching in short form. Doctrines that his movement drew from eastern religions are presented for western readers. The book's plain title promise, a broad outline, tells its scale. It is a primer of a system, not a full defence of it.
57998-on-sameness-and-identity-a-psychol:
George Stuart Fullerton wrote On Sameness and Identity, a psychological study published in April 1890 as the first number of the University of Pennsylvania's Philosophical Series. Fullerton, the university's professor of philosophy, edited the series with the psychologist James McKeen Cattell. The subtitle calls the essay a contribution to the foundations of a theory of knowledge.

The subject is basic and slippery. What makes a thing the same thing across time, and what we mean when we call two things identical, sit beneath every judgement the mind makes. The series prospectus shows the new laboratory spirit of the age: studies in progress on memory, sensation, and the rate of the nervous impulse. Fullerton's essay belongs to the moment when philosophy at American universities was remaking itself as an experimental science. It asks, with care, how the mind's sense of sameness supports everything else we claim to know.
58005-history-of-the-11th-field-company-:
The History of the 11th Field Company, Australian Engineers, was published at London in 1919. The company belonged to the Australian Imperial Force in the Great War. A dedication faces the title: to the memory of those who fell. The preface is plain about its purpose.

This little book about a little unit, it says, has been written of the company, by the company, for the company. It lays no claim to interest the outsider. It hopes only to provide a framework on which the old member can build up memories of his days in the field. A dugout's name may recall a job that cost a mate's life; a village may raise a smile at some good jest. Field companies built the war's roads, bridges, and dugouts under fire. Hundreds of such histories were printed in 1919, each a roll of names only comrades fully read.
58624-sailor-and-beachcomber-confessions:
Safroni-Middleton's Sailor and Beachcomber is subtitled confessions of a life at sea, in Australia and amid the islands of the Pacific, and was published in London by Grant Richards with illustrations. The front pages of the edition are given to the author's other trade. A catalogue of his musical compositions, printed by Boosey, fills them: marches, waltzes, and songs played by military bands throughout the world.

The catalogue carries its own witness. Lieutenant Ord Hume, the bandmaster and contest judge, is quoted calling Safroni-Middleton's military marches the finest of recent years, and unique productions from the pen of a sailor. Our Fleet, the war march of 1915, stands at the head of the list, given by special permission to Admiral Sir John Jellicoe and the British fleet. The sea life confessed in the book behind this front matter is the same life that wrote the marches.
59875-graphic-illustrations-of-abortion-:
A B Granville wrote Graphic Illustrations of Abortion and the Diseases of Menstruation. John Churchill issued the plate book at London in eighteen thirty four. Twelve plates, drawn and cut on stone, fill its wide pages. J Perry coloured each plate by hand for the grave work.

Two copper plates from the Philosophical Transactions join the set. Forty five specimens of aborted ova stand shown in all. Growths of the womb that mimic true fruit share those plates. Granville served fifteen years at the Westminster General Dispensary. Ten years at the Benevolent Lying-in Institution crown his post list. First heads fix what sound breeding is, and what marred breeding is. Conception and the ovulum’s first form take the next long span. Chorion, amnion, and the womb’s own lining fill the close study.
60471-the-busta-n-of-sadi-translated-fro:
Sadi wrote the Bustan, here Englished from the Persian in 1911. Edwards translated it with an introduction for Murray at London. The Wisdom of the East series carries the little volume. Justice, counsel, and government open its contents. A just king's counsel to his son stands first in that chapter.

A discourse concerning travellers follows in the same first chapter. Darius and a herdsman stand in its tales. Concerning benevolence opens the second chapter of the contents. Doing good to the evil is illustrated by a story there. Hatim Tai and the messenger sent to kill him stand in it. Kindness to orphans closes the second chapter's discourse list. Concerning love opens the third with a discourse on constancy. A sultan and his love for a favourite stand later in it. Sadi gives Persia its garden of counsel in verse tales.
60709-burton-island-state-park-guide-to-:
Burton Island State Park's guide to its nature and hiking trails is a Vermont pamphlet. Stephen Antil, the park naturalist, wrote and drew the book himself. Two trails start past the white cabins, behind the nature center. The nature trail takes half an hour to walk at an easy pace. Numbered posts on the path match the numbers in the pamphlet text.

The hiking trail runs one to one and a half hours in full. It leads to the southeast tip of the island and back again. Walkers are asked to wear shoes and carry out what they carry in. Wildflowers of Vermont are protected, so blooms should be left standing. The guide recalls when Iroquois and Algonquin hunted these Lake Champlain shores. Jesse Weldon cleared and tilled the island in the late seventeen hundreds. Farming stopped in 1944, and nature has since taken the land back.
61529-why-colored-people-in-philadelphia:
An anonymous pamphlet of 1866 asks why colored people in Philadelphia are excluded from the street cars, printed at Philadelphia that year. Remarks in an anti-slavery paper had implied that no efforts were made to end the exclusion. That is incorrect, the writer answers. A committee of twenty-five or thirty gentlemen was appointed at a public meeting in January of the year before. It still exists to effect the object.

The committee is evidently slow, the pamphlet owns, and has published no report, because there has been nothing good to report. Yet it has not been idle. It called on the presidents of the nineteen street railway companies and asked them to strike the excluding rule. A few favoured compliance. The rest settled on a passenger vote, and the self-respecting did not vote. The pamphlet is a reformer's prod.
62630-the-ancient-rows-of-great-yarmouth:
Lupson wrote The Ancient Rows of Great Yarmouth, a twopenny guide printed at Yarmouth in 1897. It was written for visitors, as the head of the title page declares. Its full title promises their names, why so constructed, and what visitors have written about them, with a sketch of Yarmouth beach besides. A dialect verse sings the Rows: them long bars of the gridiron that Dickens wrote on.

The text opens with the town's two surviving wonders. The two most remarkable features of the ancient borough, it says, that remain unchanged are the parish church and the Rows. The Rows are a unique series of long, narrow passages between the main streets, each numbered and named. A picture shows the entrance to row 117. Yarmouth's grid of alleys, built for a port's crowding, became its curiosity, and Lupson's pamphlet was the visitor's key to the maze.
66542-nick-carter-stories-no-138-may-1-1:
Nick Carter Stories number 138, dated May 1, 1915, came weekly from Street and Smith of New York at five cents a copy. Its tale is The Traitors of the Tropics, or Nick Carter's Royal Flush, edited by Chickering Carter. The cover matter lists subscription terms and warns readers how to send money safely.

The first chapter, A Bold Proposal, opens in a sickroom. Prince Marcos lies shot through the chest, having barely missed a puncture of the heart's sac. Dr Sloane forbids all travel. But Marcos must reach the country he rules by the eighteenth, five days off, or lose it.
69250-the-power-of-sympathy-or-the-trium:
Power of Sympathy is an early American novel by Sarah Wentworth Apthorp Morton. Walter Littlefield edited this edition, printed at Boston in 1894 in 550 copies. The first edition came from Isaiah Thomas in the year 1789. A dedication to the young ladies of United Columbia fronts the work. It vows to expose the fatal consequences of seduction to its readers.

Morton meant the tale to guard the female mind and to prize self complacency. An editor's introduction weighs the book in three kinds of value. It has antiquarian worth as a rare relic, and historical worth as well. It also shows early English novel craft in the new republic's press. Two volumes tell the tale, founded in truth by its title's claim.
69712-when-africa-awakes-the-inside-stor:
Hubert Harrison wrote When Africa Awakes, the inside story of the stirrings and strivings of Black folk. The book came out at New York with rights held in 1920, from his own press on Lenox Avenue. He gives it to those who stood by him in love, labour, and sacrifice when the foundations were laid. His portrait fronts it.

The beginnings tell of the Liberty League he launched in 1917, and of its petition to Congress. Democracy and race friction takes up the East Saint Louis horror and lynching, its cause and cure. The Negro and the war, the new politics, and the problems of leadership follow. Readers get the Harlem radical's own record.
9943-journal-of-an-expedition-into-the-i:
Lieutenant Colonel Sir Thomas Livingstone Mitchell, Surveyor-General of New South Wales, kept this journal on his expedition into tropical Australia in 1848. His aim was to find a route from Sydney to the Gulf of Carpentaria, across country then barely mapped.

The journal records daily travel, rivers, camps, and meetings with the land and its people, with maps and plates in the original edition. Mitchell writes as a surveyor and explorer, careful about distances and water. Readers get the hard, hopeful work of opening a continent's interior, day by day.
an-explanation-of-the-baltimore-catechis: Thomas L. Kinkead explains the Baltimore Catechism of Christian doctrine, with prayers, catechism, and preface, and approbations commending the book to clergy for use in schools. The work answers questions of faith in the question-and-answer form American Catholics learned by heart. It was a standard school text for generations.
doe-osti-17030341-fram-developer-trainin:
Megan Booher and Tyler Nagel of Los Alamos National Laboratory report on a fiscal year 2026 project to preserve know how for FRAM, a lab software package. Issued September 29, 2026, their report tackles a common risk: key facts about code live only in the heads of current developers. Three documentation goals structured the work.

The team documented how to set up the development environment and its known issues. They also covered the testing suite and where its gaps lie, and how the code architecture fits together module by module. Most output came as a Doxygen site, auto built from code comments into a browsable reference. Training counts and other impact measures close the report.
doe-osti-17198178-assessing-particle-ind:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-27282R closes out LDRD project 26-1402, in which Ryan M. McMullen, Michael A. Gallis, and Ross M. Wagnild asked whether dust-like particles in the air can trip a hypersonic boundary layer into turbulence. The team used direct simulation Monte Carlo, a molecular-level method, to resolve flow around particles one to ten micrometers wide. Runs covered freestream speeds from Mach 8 to 14, at flight conditions near 26 and 30 kilometers.

Companion stability calculations tracked how each particle's disturbance grows downstream. The resulting growth factors were compared with published values at which transition to turbulence occurs. The question matters because turbulent flow heats a reentry vehicle three to five times more than smooth laminar flow. The report also lays out an algorithm for two-way coupled moving surfaces in the SPARTA code, beyond the one-way coupling used in the runs shown.
doe-osti-2588657-novel-modular-treatment:
Paige Novak of the University of Minnesota led this final report for award DE-EE0009501, submitted September 16, 2025. William Arnold, Natasha Wright, and partners at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Evoqua Water Technologies share the work. The project ran from September 2021 through May 2025. It built a modular treatment system that recovers energy and reclaims water from industrial wastewater where it is produced.

The heart of the system is encapsulated biomass, anaerobic microbes sealed in protective capsules in a two-stage treatment train. Food and beverage wastewaters were the proving ground. Project publications report that community structure follows the feed type. No single keystone species drives the removal of chemical oxygen demand. Carbon-based biofilm supports improve methane yield from the encapsulated organisms. That methane is the recovered energy, drawn from waste streams factories pay to dispose of. Cost analyses weigh the modular units against conventional water recovery designs.
doe-osti-2996985-grid-reliability-and-u-:
A July 2025 guide from the Department of Energy and NARUC partnership on coal modernization briefs state regulators on what retiring coal plants mean for grid reliability. Authors Etem Erten, Beryl Taylor, and Hisham Choueiki write for the officials who must approve or delay plant closures. Coal units supply steady power and grid services that replacement resources must match.

Chapters lay out which bodies own reliability at federal, regional, and state levels. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation's 2024 long-term assessment of coal retirements is summarized, along with its advice. Later chapters catalog federal and regional tools for delaying a retirement, and state laws that have paused closures. A closing section lists the questions regulators should weigh, from replacement timing to extreme weather risk.
doe-osti-2998653-atomistic-modeling-of-t:
Wahyu Setyawan and Krishna Pitike of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report in September 2025 on computer modeling of a boundary between two materials. One side is alumina, the hard ceramic form of aluminium oxide. The other is a metal alloy, Al12Fe2Cr, whose atoms sit in a pattern close to a quasicrystal. The question was what atomic layer forms where the two meet.

The team built atom-level models and tested whether a face-centred cubic metal layer would form at the boundary. Two standard force models, MEAM and EAM, were paired with electric charge terms. For gamma alumina, both models said no such layer forms. For alpha alumina, the models disagreed, and the answer also hinged on whether the ceramic surface ended in aluminium or oxygen atoms. The work shows why test results on coated alloys can depend on the exact surface.
doe-osti-3009219-fuel-cell-hybrid-electr:
A decade-long fuel cell truck program is closed out by the Center for Transportation and the Environment under Steven Clermont. The final report for DOE award DE-EE0006523 covers July 2014 to December 2024. Partners were the University of Texas Center for Electromechanics, UPS, and Unique Electric Solutions.

The project built fuel cell hybrid electric vans for medium-duty work, trained operators, and ran field testing. Commissioning worked around missing hydrogen infrastructure. A 5,000 PSI nitrogen bottle leak-checked the hydrogen piping, and a 3,000 PSI hydrogen weld bottle fed the first fuel cell startups. A second commissioning phase followed in California, where hydrogen refuelling was available. Rooftop backup power and refuelling gear round out the scope.
doe-osti-3013762-improving-transparency-:
Natalie Mims Frick of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory prepared this slide deck, published January 16, 2026. Angela Long and Ryan Long of Rockcress Consulting worked with her. The topic is improving transparency in electric distribution system planning. Distribution planning decides which poles, wires, and substations get built. Those choices now drive a large share of household electricity bills. The deck teaches community stakeholders how the process works and where they can enter it.

Sections explain the distribution system and the utility planning steps. They cover who currently participates, and when public input can change outcomes. State examples include Michigan. There, resident comments on frequent outages pushed regulators to require better outage data from DTE. Appendices cover hosting capacity, load forecasting, and non-wires alternatives in plain terms.
doe-osti-3015665-process-optimization-an:
A University of Illinois final report under award DE-EE0009270 covers growing algae on wastewater while cleaning it. It spans October 2020 through December 2024. Georgia Tech, Buffalo, Clearas Water Recovery, and the Village of Roberts partnered. Mixed algae communities can treat effluent and yield biofuel feedstock. But swings in wastewater, weather, and microbes make output unreliable. Jeremy Guest was principal investigator.

The project attacked that control problem directly. It built design and real-time operating methods. They aim to hold effluent quality, areal productivity, and biomass composition on target at once. Plant data came through the SCADA system in five-minute intervals. The data covered energy draws from air mixing to membrane tank blowers. Daily operating logs tracked carbon dioxide fed to the photobioreactors. The stated end is commercial viability for high-rate algal treatment.
doe-osti-3020361-machine-learning-enable:
Huolin Xin's final project report for DOE award DE-SC0021204, from the University of California, Irvine, covers a project that ran from September 2020 to August 2025. The goal was to watch battery electrodes at atomic scale while they work. Xin's team built machine learning tools for electron microscopy, together with three-dimensional, cryogenic, and in-situ imaging, to reveal chemical unevenness inside lithium-ion and lithium-metal battery materials.

The group released the TEMImageNet training library and AtomSegNet models that find, sharpen, and map atoms in noisy microscope images. They also built a transfer learning model that separates mixed manganese oxidation states in spectroscopy data. Applied to all-solid-state batteries, the imaging showed failure starting at cathode-electrolyte boundaries through surface frustration and interlayer shear. The methods suit beam-sensitive materials that ordinary microscopy damages.
doe-osti-3020681-energy-to-communities-p:
Slide deck by Hannah Pauling of NLR, dated December 2025, introduces DOE's Energy to Communities (E2C) program through one project. The project evaluates an enhanced geothermal system to heat Cornell University's campus district heating network. E2C pairs communities with national laboratory analysts for in-depth partnerships lasting about three years, or shorter peer-learning cohorts, before technology is deployed.

The technical core is a 30-year reservoir simulation run with the Waiwera simulator. The modeled system uses wells 3.5 kilometers deep, spaced 500 meters apart, in rock at 100 degrees Celsius. Water is injected at 50 degrees Celsius at 55 kilograms per second through a 400-meter fracture zone. The slides show pressure and temperature results used to refine well configuration and flow rate. They also outline the wider E2C offer: modeling, hardware simulation, and planning support for local energy goals.
doe-osti-3025381-cdte-core-final-technic:
Matthew Reese of the National Laboratory of the Rockies closes the CdTe Core program in report NLR/TP-5K00-99142, dated March 2026. Cadmium telluride is a leading thin-film solar material, and a core program's job is the shared science underneath commercial cell making: contacts, buffers, and interfaces. Small misalignments between layers quietly tax every cell the industry ships.

One thread concerns the transparent front contact. Tin oxide stacks, including the commercial Pilkington TEC12D product, are common, air-stable superstrate materials, and buffers such as magnesium zinc oxide are added on top. Cadmium telluride alone aligns poorly with tin oxide bands, which has long been a problem. Alloying the absorber with selenium bends the bands more favorably, though the report notes the alignment is still not ideal, and optimized processing works around the gap.
doe-osti-3025690-overview-of-nlr-automat:
J Sam Lott of Automated Mobility Services LLC, with Stanley Young and Andrew Duvall of the National Laboratory of the Rockies. They sum up three phases of automated mobility district research in report NLR/TP-5400-97559, dated March 2026. This third edition argues that automation, electrification, and on-demand service converge in districts: bounded areas where driverless shuttles can be introduced under controlled, resilient conditions.

Practical guardrails fill the middle sections. Operators are advised to limit automated vehicles to dedicated lanes. They should run at lower speeds even in mixed traffic, and keep safety attendants aboard to handle the tough spots and give passengers a human authority. Fleets should be remotely monitored from an operations center. Vehicle sensors can be augmented by intelligent roadway infrastructure, roadside sensing and communications that widen what each vehicle knows.
doe-osti-3362834-unalakleet-microgrid-op:
Reese Huhta of the Unalakleet Valley Electric Cooperative reports final results for the Unalakleet Native Corporation under award DE-IE0000112, dated April 30, 2026. Total costs came to about 1.26 million dollars, with a federal share near 670,000 dollars. Unalakleet, an Alaska Native community of about 745 people, sits off the road system. It relies on its own wind-diesel microgrid. The grid runs four diesel generators of 475 kilowatts each. Six wind turbines add 100 kilowatts apiece.

The optimization project tuned how that grid runs day to day. Outage counts fell 44 percent from 2024 to 2025, from 23 events to 13, and total outage time fell 72 percent, from 462 minutes to 130. The share of outages under one minute nearly doubled, to 69 percent. Lessons cover controls, maintenance, and keeping local energy sources at the center.
doe-osti-3375176-cybermesa-evaluation-pr:
Report INL/RPT-25-88240 from Idaho National Laboratory, dated December 2025, sets out CyberMESA, a scored test method for the cyber safety of vehicle charging gear. Kenneth Rohde and Richard “Barney” Carlson of Idaho lead the author list. Staff from Pacific Northwest and the National Laboratory of the Rockies fill out a ten-person team. Charging networks mix gear from many makers, run by many firms. That sprawl makes blanket rules such as IEC 62443 hard to enforce end to end.

CyberMESA instead grades single devices, starting with the charger itself. Each check has a fixed script and a point scale. One test times the SSH login grace window on a charger. A long window gives password guessing more room, so it scores worse. The aim is a shared yardstick that vendors can design against and buyers can trust.
doe-osti-3375699-strong-marine-hydrogen-:
A Period I final project report dated November 2025 covers the Marine Hydrogen Demonstration on the San Francisco waterfront. Hornblower Energy LLC was the prime recipient. Narendra Pal, chief of Pacific Hydrogen LLC, led the work. Air Liquide, Bayotech, Sandia National Laboratories, and the Port of San Francisco partnered on it. The funding came through the Energy Department's H2@Scale program. The aim was shore-side hydrogen supply for the bay's fuel cell ferries.

The team had run the Sea Change ferry in city service. That boat proved the tech, but fueling stayed ad hoc. This project designed a hydrogen barge and a formal refueling protocol. Flow studies checked tank heating during a forty-five minute fill. With the picked injector, gas leaves at about 157 meters per second. Tank heat then spreads evenly, peaking near eighty degrees Celsius. Those marks clear the team's safety bar.
doe-osti-3376043-integrating-resilience-:
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report, published June 29, 2026, argues for weaving resilience into the standard plans utilities file for their distribution grids. Its authors are Myles Collins, Arthur Mallet Dias, Lisa Schwartz, and Paul De Martini. Storms, fires, and heat now break local grids more often. Yet many plans still treat resilience as a side note. The report shows planners how to weigh resilience work beside the usual wires and poles choices, with clear cost tests.

Two yardsticks get a close read. One picks the cheapest plan that still meets set legal and safety bars. It never asks if the gains top the cost. The other, benefit-cost analysis, puts all gains and costs in dollars over a set span. That shared unit makes the trade plain to read. The report sorts which drivers call for which test, and how to keep the sums honest.
doe-osti-3683724-powering-large-loads-so:
Sandia report SAND2026-25780, printed August 2026, surveys ways to power very large new electricity loads. Raquel Valdez and Thushara Gunda are the two printed authors. Demand is rising fast in many regions, driven in part by data centres and new industry. No single fix fits, so the report sorts options by the level where they act. Tables list each option's main actors, rough timelines, and limits.

At the transmission level, options span new lines and grid-enhancing tools. At the utility level, they cover planning and programme routes. At the facility level, they reach on-site supply and load shaping. Shared patterns then come under review. Build options often stall on permits, land review, and supply chains. Running options lean on sound data, clear rules, and customer buy-in. Planners must also weigh building too little against stranded plant if loads never show.
doe-osti-3715527-multi-ignition-fire-com: A short highlight sheet from the Office of Science, dated January 12, 2026, sums up a study of merging wildfires. Qi Tang, James Randerson, and co-authors sorted satellite fire images in California and northern forests by whether starts stayed single or merged. Merged complexes drove the worst fire years, made more fire-storm clouds, and split crews across fronts. A high-resolution run of the 2020 Dixie fire showed how twin updrafts whip up shifting surface winds. The work appeared in Science Advances.
govdocs-archive_org-WRNFEuropeanCommisio:
Harlan Cleveland and Marc Luyckx wrote Religion and Governance as a joint paper of the World Academy of Art and Science and the European Commission's Forward Studies Unit. They presented it at the Brussels Seminar on Governance and Civilizations, held May 14 to 16, 1998.

The paper asks how religion will shape government and foreign policy in the twenty-first century, a question European planners were taking up as the Cold War order faded. It treats faith not as a fading force but as a rising factor in world politics. Readers get a policy paper from the moment before that prediction was widely tested.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAFilesDestruc:
Harold Weisberg's lawsuits forced more assassination paper into the open than anyone else's, and this 1976 filing is the government answering him. In Weisberg v. GSA, the United States Attorney's office, under Earl J. Silbert, opposed his motion in federal court in Washington.

Weisberg had moved to restrain the CIA from destroying documents, and the government opposed the restraint. The stakes were real, since the agency had destroyed records before and researchers feared for what remained. Court filings like this one are the legal record of the fight over whether the assassination archive would survive at all.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAKirkpatrickL:
Lyman Kirkpatrick had been the CIA's inspector general, and his book The Real CIA was an insider's defense of the agency. This note, dated December 29, 1972, was written by a reader who was not persuaded, and who did not sign the critique.

The note attacks Kirkpatrick's picture of the agency, taking up his claim about its real purpose being a state of perpetual self-reorganization, and treating the book as an apologia. Marginal warfare like this filled the files of the intelligence debate: readers grading the insiders' memoirs line by line. The single note is preserved as a specimen of that argument.
journal-of-an-expedition-into-the-interi:
Thomas Livingstone Mitchell's journal tells of his expedition into the interior of tropical Australia. He searched for a route from Sydney to the Gulf of Carpentaria. Mitchell was surveyor-general of New South Wales. The Legislative Council petitioned for the expedition, and the colony paid its costs. His journal, dated 1848 in the title, is dedicated to that council.

Mitchell's preface praises Australia's interior as a field for philosopher, painter, poet, and naturalist. No ruined cities reward the traveler there, he admits. Instead he finds signs of healthful progress and hope. The journal follows his party through unknown country, recording land, water, and prospects for settlement. It is a founding document of Australian exploration, written by the colony's chief surveyor.
nasa-tm-19660020115-progress-and-problem:
Alfred J Eggers Jr and Nathaniel B Cohen, of NASA's Office of Advanced Research and Technology, surveyed entry into atmospheres in Athens in September 1965. Entry problems are motion, heating, and heat protection, the abstract says. Their setting is present and future space flight. Uncrewed probes to Mars, Venus, and Jupiter are considered alongside crewed vehicles built for controlled planetary entry and return.

Every world with air presents the same three problems in new forms. A survey at that date could draw on early probe and capsule flights. It could also point at the gaps that later missions would have to close. Eggers and Cohen give program leaders a shared map of a field that every deep space plan depends on.
nasa-tm-19680018063-the-significance-of-:
Harleth G. Wiley of Langley Research Center examines nonlinear damping trends for current aircraft in this paper, presented in Cambridge in September 1966. Damping describes how quickly an aircraft settles after a pitch or yaw disturbance. Engineers measure it in wind tunnels with a rigidly forced dynamic stability technique.

Wiley reviews the basic features and accuracy of that Langley technique. It works across subsonic, transonic, and supersonic speeds. The method also permits tests at high angles of attack. He then weighs what the nonlinear trends mean for real aircraft configurations. The paper helps engineers judge how much trust to place in tunnel damping data.
nasa-tm-19690011513-electrothermal-insta:
J. Marlin Smith of Lewis Research Center studies unstable flow at the mouth of an MHD power unit in this report. Such units turn hot flowing gas straight into electric power. At the mouth of one type, electron heat rises fast. Electron counts then climb by four or five orders of size.

Smith checks if that steep rise zone stays stable. Past work assumed a uniform, endless gas, which the mouth zone is not. His answer assumes one field stays small beside the applied field. The zone proved stable with no magnet field in place. With a magnet field applied, the same zone proved unstable.
nasa-tm-19690026900-individual-angular-m:
Hans F. Kennel, of the Astrionics Laboratory at Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this January 1968 memorandum, TM X-53696. Three double-gimbaled control moment gyros form the actuators for one steering mode of the Apollo Telescope Mount. Tilting their spinning wheels steers the mount without thrusters. Kennel develops laws for sharing and rotating the wheels' momentum.

Left alone, two momentum vectors can drift parallel while the third points opposite, he warns. That bad spread cuts the total momentum available to one third. His distribution law instead settles the vectors at equal angles, an arrangement he calls isogonal. It avoids the bad case, maximizes control gain, and minimizes cross coupling. A rotation law then keeps inner gimbals off their stops, even after one gyro fails.
nasa-tm-19700025195-postflight-analysis-:
Apollo 6 radar tracking data get a postflight analysis in this Houston internal note, dated September 13, 1968. Apollo 6 was an uncrewed test flight of the Saturn 5 rocket and the Apollo command module. The note checks how well the ground navigation system had followed the flight.

The analyses tested the unified S-band system's orbit determination skill against C-band radar results. The two systems agreed excellently, the summary reports, but the work uncovered a serious fault in Ascension range data. Odd tugs on the spacecraft's path were traced to water boiling off and venting. The authors warn that the water boiler could seriously affect future missions if left unchecked.
nasa-tm-19710007101-pumping-characterist:
Sol H. Gorland and James C. Wood of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in January 1971. It measures how a spinning cone with its tip cut off acts as a pump. The part tested was the conical rotor of a Lundell-type alternator, run as a pump for the study.

The cone was spun at speeds up to tens of thousands of turns each minute. Head and flow readings were taken across that range. The authors found that equations for enclosed rotating disks could predict the behavior well. Such rotors move coolant inside space power systems, where a plain, reliable pump is prized.
nasa-tm-19720006493-use-of-radiation-in-:
W H Philipp, S J Marsik, C E May, and R A Lad of the Lewis Research Center summed up their radiation chemistry work in December 1971, as NASA TM X-67982. They used radiation to prepare pure materials, above all clean metals. A beam of fast electrons drove chemical changes in solutions. The paper updates their earlier published results. It also explains the reaction paths behind the method.

Their main process reduced dissolved metal salts to the free metal. It worked from water solutions for a long list of metals. Copper, silver, iron, nickel, and palladium were among them. The team also tested dry organic liquids as the working fluid. Those trials included making water free metal halides.
of-the-orthographie-and-congruitie-of-th:
Alexander Hume, a schoolmaster, wrote this treatise on English spelling. Its full title calls it a treatise for the schools. Henry Wheatley edited it from a British Museum manuscript. The Early English Text Society printed it in 1865. The preface says the tract was then printed first.

Hume sets rules for spelling and for correct sentence structure. The old spelling of the title shows the problem he faced. English then had no single fixed standard for writing. His rules aimed to help teachers and pupils. The work helps readers trace early spelling reform. Wheatley printed it from the original manuscript for scholars.
the-abolitionists-together-with-personal: John F. Hume wrote The Abolitionists, with personal memories of the struggle for human rights from 1830 to 1864, printed by G. P. Putnam's Sons of New York and London in 1905. Chapters listed cover Theodore Roosevelt and the abolitionists, anti-slavery pioneers, Salmon Portland Chase, John Quincy Adams, anti-slavery societies and orators, Lincoln and Douglas, anti-slavery women, mobs, and anti-slavery martyrs.
the-pearl-a-middle-english-poem-a-modern: Sophie Jewett, associate professor of English literature at Wellesley College, made a modern version of The Pearl, a Middle English poem, in the metre of the original. Her version appeared in 1908 and is dedicated to Katharine Lee Bates. Only the front matter is present here, so the poem itself does not appear. Jewett addresses a verse apology to the unknown medieval poet, and lists earlier editions by Morris, Gollancz, and Osgood, with other translations.
what-all-the-world-s-a-seeking-the-vital:
Ralph Waldo Trine wrote What All the World's A-Seeking, a short book on the laws of a true and happy life. The Dodge company of New York printed it. Trine says in his preface that the time felt ripe for the book. It came, he adds, from his heart to reach the hearts of others.

A later preface tells of letters from grateful readers around the world. For the revised edition Trine added a part on thought power and character, about thirty pages long. It answers the questions readers asked most. The book urges people to build a strong, calm inner life. Its tone is warm, earnest, and hopeful.
